questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman traveled to West Africa for a year-long research project. A few weeks into her trip she began to notice strange dreams followed by a paranoid feeling of people following her.
questions.lead_in: What prophylactic agent is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Mefloquine A variety of neuropsychiatric side effects of mefloquine are well described. In particular, strange dreams and sensations of paranoia are among the most frequent.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q8

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman sought travel advice for a 1-week trip to Zambia. Her departure date was in 1 month. She was 16-weeks pregnant. She intended to visit friends and relatives. She was given advice regarding mosquito bite avoidance.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate malaria chemoprophylaxis?

options.text: Medical prophylaxis contraindicated due to pregnancy

questions.explanation: Mefloquine Pregnancy is a risk factor for severe disease in malaria, and pregnant women are advised to avoid travel to malarious areas. However, if travel cannot be avoided, then prophylaxis for malaria should be offered to all patients traveling to areas at risk. Although chloroquine is safe in all trimesters of pregnancy, resistance in Plasmodium falciparum is widespread, and mefloquine is the only other medication shown to be safe for use during pregnancy and that remains active in most areas. Doxycycline and atovaquone–proguanil should not be used in pregnancy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q43

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman attended for pretravel advice. She was planning a 1-week trip to Haiti. She was 25 weeks pregnant, and it was her first pregnancy.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate malaria prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: Chloroquine Malaria prophylaxis is indicated as Haiti is considered at moderate risk for acquisition of malaria. Although Plasmodium falciparum accounts for almost all cases of malaria in Haiti, resistance is exceedingly rare. In addition, the patient is pregnant, and the only medication that is considered safe from the above list is chloroquine. Atovaquone–proguanil, artemether–lumefantrine, and doxycycline are contraindicated regardless of the trimester. Mosquito bite avoidance is extremely important, and suitable precautions must be discussed. She should also be advised that national recommendations (both CDC and the PHE Advisory Committee on Malaria Prevention) are that pregnant women should avoid all nonessential travel to malarious areas due to the increased risk of severe malaria and death or serious adverse outcomes such as stillbirth and miscarriage.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q33

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman attended clinic for pretravel counseling. She was 18 weeks pregnant. She was planning a 2-week holiday to Kenya to visit her husband. It was her first pregnancy and had been uneventful to date. She was taking prenatal vitamins and was allergic to penicillin (rash only). She was given advice on mosquito bite avoidance and insect repellent.
questions.lead_in: What would be the most appropriate malaria chemo prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: Mefloquine Mefloquine is the drug of choice for prophylaxis in the setting of pregnancy. Clindamycin is not an adequate drug for malaria chemoprophylaxis. Hydroxychloroquine and doxycycline should not be used during pregnancy due to teratogenic effects. Atovaquone–proguanil has emerging data for use during pregnancy, but mefloquine remains the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis during pregnancy. If travel is essential, the risk of any prophylactic drug in pregnancy has to be weighed against the risk of contracting malaria. However, do not forget that pregnant women should be advised to avoid traveling to malarial areas; pregnant women are at higher risk of severe malaria, and malaria increases the risk of adverse fetal outcomes, including premature birth and stillbirth.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q31

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man attended clinic for a pretravel review. He had a history of hypertension controlled with enalapril. He had no known drug allergies. He was planning a 4-week trip to the Middle East. He had previously taken chloroquine and had tolerated it well and was keen to use that again if possible.

questions.question: 17.  Severe malaria in Canadian traveller.  Has Hb 65. Sao2 of 85%. Confused and GCS 9. Falciparum parasitemia of 6%.

parts.text: A.  What criteria does he have for severe disease?
B.  What is the histopathologic feature of cerebral malaria?
C.  What are four other criteria for severe disease?
D.  What is the treatment?

cohort_answer.text:
Parasetemia >5% in non-immune for >5yo; Hb <70; ARDS; Impaired conciousness
Sequestration of infected RBCs in brain microvasculature, ring haemorrhages
IV artesunate for at least 24 hours then complete therapy with a course of atovaquone-proguanil

questions.question: Patient who traveled to India and Cambodia. Malaria prophylaxis with Mefloquine. Sx severe malaria and positive rapid test when returning to Canada.

parts.text: Which Plasmodium species is most likely involved?
Explain why?
What is the place of acquisition?
Name two treatments (first and second line)
Explain why first-line treatment is better
How to monitor the potential emergence of resistance to first-line treatment?

cohort_answer.text:
Species: P. falciparum
Why: Falciparum & vivax sp are found in both countries but falciparum is the only one that typically causes severe malaria. Known mefloquine resistance in Cambodia.
Place of acquisition: Cambodia (has areas of Mefloquine resistance)
Treatments: Parentral Artesunate; Parentral Quinine + clinda
Why first-line better: Rapid activity, clears parasitemia faster; Activity against all erythrocytic stages of the parasite; Minimal resistance; Very well tolerated, less adverse effects compared to quinine (eg hypoglycaemia); Easy to administer; No dose adjustment for organ impairment; No significant drug interactions; Does not require cardiac monitoring. Disadvantages: Short half life <2hrs therefore can relapse if not given an oral course as step down; Can cause delayed haemolysis (weekly CBCs x 4 weeks)
Monitoring resistance: Repeat blood smears to monitor clearance of parasitemia – if delayed, may have resistance

questions.question: A healthy man is traveling to Honduras (chloroquine sensitive) and requires malaria prophylaxis.

parts.text: Name 4 options for malaria prophylaxis, and indicate when to start and to stop for each (table: Prophylactic agent, start, stop)

questions.model_answer: 4 options for a chloroquine-sensitive destination (Honduras): (1) Chloroquine - start 1-2 weeks before travel, take weekly during travel, continue for 4 weeks after leaving. (2) Atovaquone-proguanil - start 1-2 days before travel, take daily during travel, continue for 7 days after leaving. (3) Doxycycline - start 1-2 days before travel, take daily during travel, continue for 4 weeks after leaving. (4) Mefloquine - start 2-3 weeks before travel, take weekly during travel, continue for 4 weeks after leaving.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC Yellow Book malaria chemoprophylaxis timing recommendations.

questions.question: In the following examples, please give examples of drugs or drug classes that prolong QT (You can only use the same class once)

parts.text: 2 antibacterial
1 antiviral
1 antiparasitic
1 antimycobacterial

questions.model_answer:
(1) Antibacterial (2 classes): macrolides (e.g., azithromycin/clarithromycin/erythromycin) and fluoroquinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin).
(2) Antiviral: ritonavir (or other protease inhibitors).
(3) Antiparasitic: chloroquine (or quinine).
(4) Antimycobacterial: bedaquiline (or clofazimine).
questions.cites: Mandell p. 265 (general knowledge for non-macrolide classes; macrolide QT effect Mandell p. 268)
questions.beyond_mandell: Non-macrolide QT-prolonging examples (fluoroquinolones, ritonavir, chloroquine, bedaquiline) reflect general pharmacology/product labeling rather than this chapter's text.

questions.question: 24yo with recent travel to Malawi, reports he was treated 10 days ago there for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria with artemisinin-lumefantrine x 3 days. Feeling well.

parts.text: RDT is positive for P falciparum (no smear given). Give 4 reasons for this result.
Thick and thin smear shows only gametocytes for P falciparum, B/W otherwise normal apart from anemia. Would you treat again and give a reason. No travel planned in the next year.
Give two regimens for treating uncomplicated falciparum malaria available in Canada

questions.model_answer: a) Four reasons for positive RDT at day 10: (1) persistent HRP-2 antigenemia despite parasite clearance (can persist weeks) (2) residual circulating gametocytes (3) true recrudescence/treatment failure (4) reinfection (unlikely, no further travel). b) Would not retreat: gametocytes alone (without asexual forms) on smear with a well-appearing, otherwise normal patient reflects post-treatment gametocytemia, not treatment failure - gametocytes are not affected by most blood schizonticides and can persist for weeks without indicating ongoing infection or transmission risk to self. c) Two regimens for uncomplicated falciparum available in Canada: artemether-lumefantrine, and atovaquone-proguanil (quinine plus doxycycline is an alternative).

questions.question: Middle-aged person is going to Honduras for vacation. He/she requires malaria prophylaxis.

parts.text: List 4 regimens that can be used. You can assuming he/she will require prophylaxis for the entire trip

questions.model_answer: 4 regimens usable for the entire trip to a chloroquine-sensitive area (Honduras): (1) chloroquine, (2) atovaquone-proguanil, (3) doxycycline, (4) mefloquine.

questions.question: Kid traveled in Africa, present with fever 39.5, RR30, sat 85%, parasitemia 6%, confusion/Glasgow 9

parts.text: 4 criteria of severe malaria in this case
4 other criteria of severe malaria
Best treatment
Parasitemia down to 2% at D2, 1% at D3. Do you consider this as therapeutic success

cohort_answer.text: 4 criteria of severe malaria in this case: Parasitemia 6% (in non-immune); Resp: SpO2 85%; GCS 9; ?confusion. Best treatment: IV artesunate. Therapeutic success: Yes

questions.question: Travel returning from India via Cambodia (stayed there several days – no clear timeline given during trip) had been on mefloquine prophylaxis and adherent, now 7 days post return with fevers and + malaria RDT.

parts.text: a) what is pathogen and where was it acquired?
b) Recommended treatment and 1 alternative
c) What are the advantages to this regimen
d) What should you monitor for?

cohort_answer.text:
Mefloquine-resistant P falciparum - Cambodia. (P vivax - Africa/Asia/South Pacific/Central-South America, possible but mefloquine resistance low unless Papua New Guinea; P ovale unlikely, endemic W Africa rarely SE Asia; P malariae exists in SEA but mefloquine sensitive/infrequent). RDTs: HRP2 targets P falciparum only, LDH and Aldolase pan-plasmodium
(Assuming NOT severe) Oral Artemisinin combination therapy (ACT); Malarone; Quinine + Clinda/Doxy. If severe: artesunate 2.4mg/kg 0,12,24,48hr + clindamycin or doxycycline or malarone; Alternative: Quinine 5.8mg/kg PLUS malarone/doxy/clinda
Mortality benefit with artesunate; oral/rectal options; dual treatment decreases treatment failure; less side effects; quicker drop in malaria load, kills all stages; low resistance rates
Parasite density typically daily until negative; if artesunate used, monitor weekly CBC for delayed hemolysis (up to 4 weeks after). Artesunate preferred: IV form, mortality benefit. Resistance suspected if recrudescence/parasite density does not drop

questions.question: AM 9. Malaria - name 4 drug options for chemoprophylaxis in person going to Honduras and when to start and to stop assuming that they are required for the entire duration of travel (4)

parts.text: Name 4 drug options with start/stop timing

cohort_answer.text: Malarone - start 1-2 days prior to exposure, continue 1 week post return. Doxycycline - start 1-2 days prior, continue 4 weeks post return. Mefloquine - start minimum 1 week prior (ideally 2-3), continue 4 weeks post return. Chloroquine - start 1-2 weeks prior, continue 4 weeks post return.

questions.question: A youngish man was in Malawi and was diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum. He was treated with artemether-lumefantrine. He was rechecked by his doctor in Canada 10 days later with a rapid diagnostic test and thick and thin smears. The rapid test was positive.

parts.text: What are four reasons why the test could be positive for this patient?
The thick and thin smears show only gametocytes on 2 of 3 smears. He is not planning on travelling anywhere for the next year. What do you tell him regarding treatment (2)?
What are 2 treatment regimens for uncomplicated malaria from this region that you could use? Medication options must be mutually exclusive.

questions.model_answer: a) Four reasons for persistent positive RDT: persistent HRP-2 antigenemia after cure, residual gametocytes, true recrudescence, or reinfection. b) With only gametocytes on smear and no further travel: no retreatment needed - gametocytes represent residual sexual-stage parasites, not ongoing/failed infection, and pose no transmission risk in a non-endemic setting without a competent vector; reassurance and clinical follow-up is appropriate. c) Two mutually exclusive regimens for uncomplicated falciparum from this region: artemether-lumefantrine OR atovaquone-proguanil.

questions.question: Identify agents of each class that cause QTc prolongation (cannot reuse the same agent): 2 antibiotics, 1 antiparasitic, 1 anti-TB

parts.text: 2 antibiotics causing QTc prolongation
1 antiparasitic causing QTc prolongation
1 anti-TB drug causing QTc prolongation

cohort_answer.text: Antibiotics: Ciprofloxacin, Azithromycin. Antiparasitic: Quinine, Sodium stibogluconate, Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine (also possible but rare ~5%). Anti-TB: Clofazimine, Bedaquiline, Linezolid.

parts.text: 2 antibiotics
1 antiparasitic

cohort_answer.text: 2 antibiotics: Macrolides (Azithromycin), Fluroquinolones (Levofloxacin, Ciprofloxacin). 1 antiparasitic: Quinine, Chloroquine, Mefloquine. 1 anti-TB: Bedaquiline, Clofazimine.

parts.text: List 4 malaria prophylaxis options including instructions on when to start and when to stop

cohort_answer.text: Chloroquine 500mg salt PO 1-2 weeks prior to leaving, then weekly while there, then continue weekly for 4 weeks after returning. Mefloquine 250mg salt PO weekly 2-3 weeks prior to leaving, weekly while away then for 4 weeks after returning. Atovaquone/proguanil 250mg/100mg PO daily 1-2 days before leaving, daily while away, then for 1 week after returning. Doxycycline 100mg PO daily 1-2 days before leaving, daily while away, then 4 weeks after returning
